title: Single Number II
statement:
In the integer array `nums`, one value occurs exactly once and every other value occurs exactly three times. Return the value that occurs once.

Your solution must run in linear time and use only a constant amount of extra memory.
constraints: Exactly one value of nums appears once; every other value appears exactly three times
notes:
## Intuition

Counting each value in a hash map finds the loner easily, but uses O(n) memory. Think per bit instead: for every bit position, the values seen three times contribute a multiple of three set bits, so the count of ones at that bit, taken modulo 3, is exactly the single value's bit. Two words, `ones` and `twos`, can hold that count modulo 3 for all 32 bits at once: a bit is set in `ones` when its count so far is 1 (mod 3), set in `twos` when it is 2, and clear in both when it is 0.

## Approach

1. Start with `ones = 0` and `twos = 0` (every bit has count 0).
2. For each `num`, update `ones` first: `ones ^ num` adds the bits of `num`, and `& ~twos` drops any bit that was already at count 2, because its count is now 3 and wraps to 0.
3. Then update `twos` with the new `ones`: `twos ^ num` advances the bits, and `& ~ones` keeps only bits that did not just land in `ones`. A bit moves 0 → 1 → 2 → 0 as it is seen.
4. After all numbers, every tripled value has cycled back to 0, so `ones` holds exactly the single value.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 2, 3, 2]` (binary `10, 10, 11, 10`).

- `num = 2`: `ones = 2`, `twos = 0`.
- `num = 2`: `ones = (2 ^ 2) & ~0 = 0`, `twos = (0 ^ 2) & ~0 = 2`.
- `num = 3`: `ones = (0 ^ 3) & ~2 = 1`, `twos = (2 ^ 3) & ~1 = 0`.
- `num = 2`: `ones = (1 ^ 2) & ~0 = 3`, `twos = (0 ^ 2) & ~3 = 0`.

The answer is `ones = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): two bitwise updates per number.
- Space: O(1): just `ones` and `twos`.

## Pitfalls

- XOR of everything (the trick for Single Number I) does not work: three copies XOR to the value itself, not to 0.
- Order matters: update `ones` first, then `twos` using the new `ones`.
- Negative numbers are fine because the bitwise operators work on the 32-bit two's-complement form; a per-bit counting version in other languages must rebuild the sign bit correctly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ones` | bits whose count so far is 1 modulo 3 |
| `twos` | bits whose count so far is 2 modulo 3 |
| `num` | the value being added |

narration.2: ones marks every bit seen once (modulo 3) so far.
narration.3: twos marks every bit seen twice (modulo 3) so far.
narration.4: Feed in the numbers one at a time.
narration.5: Toggle num's bits into ones, but not bits already in twos: those reach a count of three and reset.
narration.6: Toggle num's bits into twos, except those that just landed in ones.
narration.8: Every value seen three times has cycled back to zero, so ones holds the single value.
